analysis.one_liner: Triples inspections of gun dealers, raises penalties for recordkeeping violations, and lets ATF revoke problem dealers' licenses.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 24, 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill has had no committee vote or floor action since, and none of its ten sponsors or cosponsors is a Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten oversight of federally licensed gun dealers. It would let the ATF (the federal agency that regulates gun sellers) inspect any dealer up to three times a year instead of once, hire 80 more inspectors, deny licenses to applicants who pose a public safety risk, and suspend or revoke a dealer's license or impose fines of up to $10,000 per violation. It would also raise prison terms for false statements in required gun records from one year to five years, and up to ten years when the false records relate to unlawful gun transfers.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by gun trafficking and violence, and law-abiding buyers, would gain from stronger checks on the small share of licensed dealers that supply illegal gun markets. A dealer who loses track of guns that later turn up at crime scenes could be forced to run a full physical inventory, making it easier to catch diversion of guns to criminals.

how_it_helps.text: The ATF could deny a federal firearms license if issuing it would endanger public safety or the applicant is unlikely to comply with the law.
Dealers could be inspected up to three times a year instead of once, and the ATF could hire at least 80 additional employees to conduct the extra inspections.
The ATF could suspend or revoke a dealer's license, or impose a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, for violating federal firearms laws — powers that currently require far narrower grounds.
If a dealer unlawfully transfers a firearm, or ten or more guns used in crimes are traced back to that dealer, the ATF could require a full physical inventory and a detailed inventory record.

The maximum prison term for knowingly making a false statement in required firearms records rises from one year to five years, and to ten years when tied to unlawful gun transfers or trafficking-related offenses.

analysis.who_pays: Federally licensed firearms dealers bear the cost: more frequent inspections, possible fines of $10,000 per violation, license suspensions or revocations, mandatory physical inventories, and heavier criminal exposure for recordkeeping violations. Taxpayers fund the additional 80 inspector positions.

drawbacks.text: Dealers would face up to three inspections a year, fines of up to $10,000 per violation, and license suspension or revocation for violating any federal firearms law or regulation, a compliance burden that falls hardest on small independent shops.

The ATF could deny a license application it judges a danger to public safety, 'not likely to comply with the law,' or 'otherwise not suitable' — broad standards whose application would depend heavily on which administration runs the agency.
The bill strikes the 'willfully' requirement from licensing penalty provisions and raises maximum prison terms, so recordkeeping errors could carry substantially heavier consequences than today.
The authority to hire at least 80 additional ATF employees is not paired with dedicated funding, so Congress would need to appropriate the money for the added inspections to actually happen.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and documented pathway for guns to reach people prohibited from having them: a minority of licensed dealers who sell illegally or keep sloppy records. The benefits — fewer crime guns on the street — are spread broadly across communities, while the costs — inspection time, fines, and heavier penalties — fall on a specific industry, and small dealers would feel them most. Honest supporters acknowledge the bill gives the ATF wide discretion over who gets to sell guns at all, which makes its effect depend on how future administrations use it; the bill's own hearing and court-review provisions offer dealers some recourse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no committee vote and no floor action, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Representative Seth Magaziner introduced the bill in the House on June 24, 2025, joined by six original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, its only action to date.
Nine Democratic cosponsors have signed on; no Republican has.
No committee markup, vote, or floor action has occurred since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federally licensed firearms dealers are better off so far, because none of the added inspections, penalties, or license-revocation powers has moved any closer to taking effect.

for.name: Seth Magaziner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six original cosponsors.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for any committee consideration since its referral.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits with the Republican-chaired House Judiciary Committee, which has not acted on it.

industries.note: Dealers would face tripled inspections, fines of up to $10,000 per violation, license suspension or revocation, mandatory inventories when crime guns trace back to them, and up to ten years in prison for recordkeeping tied to unlawful transfers. Their interest in this bill runs against stricter enforcement of the rules meant to keep guns away from people barred from buying them.

Manufacturers and importers could also be ordered to run full physical inventories if crime guns trace back to them or if they unlawfully transfer a firearm, though the bill's heaviest burdens fall on retail dealers. Sales to compliant dealers would be unaffected.

analysis.trajectory: With the House controlled by Republicans, the bill sitting in the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee with no Republican cosponsor, and no committee action for months, it is very unlikely to get a vote this Congress unless its backers find Republican support or attach it to larger legislation.
